claims.text: Controlled annealing of pre-exposure Q235 steel promotes formation of a uniform nanocrystalline passive oxide film.
The annealing-induced passive film significantly enhances Q235 corrosion protection at room temperature.
The annealing-induced passive film significantly enhances Q235 corrosion protection during aggressive-salt exposure at 700–900 °C.
As-received pre-exposure Q235 steel has heterogeneous oxide coverage.
As-received pre-exposure Q235 steel has a heterogeneous microstructure.
Annealing at approximately 800 °C can refine the microstructure of Q235 steel.
Annealing at approximately 800 °C under an inert or controlled atmosphere can produce a uniform passive film on Q235 steel.
Annealing drives thermomechanical evolution that produces grain refinement and a homogeneous oxide scale.
A fine, coherent, uniform nanocrystalline oxide layer acts as a corrosion barrier by reducing defect-related corrosion pathways.
The uniform passive film mitigates localized degradation during thermal cycling.
Heterogeneous oxide distribution on untreated Q235 predisposes it to localized corrosion.
Heterogeneous oxide distribution on untreated Q235 predisposes it to high-temperature scale spallation.
Annealed Q235 will exhibit lower mass loss than untreated Q235 under room- and high-temperature corrosive exposure.
Annealed Q235 will exhibit less oxide-scale spallation than untreated Q235.
Annealed Q235 will exhibit greater electrochemical stability than untreated Q235.
Untreated Q235 has a nonuniform passive film and higher corrosion rates under the specified exposures.
The proposed protection requires annealing conditions that limit excessive oxidation.
Excessive oxidation during annealing would prevent the proposed protection mechanism from applying.
The mechanism may not extend to steels with substantially different alloying compositions.
The mechanism may not apply to steels with prior surface treatments that already produce stable passive films.
